title: Ὁδοιπόρος καὶ Ἑρμῆς
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 260. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὁδοιπόρος πολλὴν ὁδὸν ἀνύων ηὔξατο, ἐὰν εὕρῃ τι, τούτου τὸ ἥμισυ τῷ Ἑρμῇ ἀναθήσειν.
sentences.tr: Hodoiporos pollēn hodon anyōn ēuxato, ean heurēi ti, toutou to hēmisy tōi Hermēi anathēsein.
sentences.l: A traveller accomplishing a long road vowed that, if he should find anything, he would dedicate the half of it to Hermes.
sentences.n: Hermes is the god of the lucky find — a windfall is an ἕρμαιον, 'a thing of Hermes' — so a vow over whatever one may pick up on the road belongs to him. The vow keeps the mood the man himself used: ἐάν with the subjunctive εὕρῃ, where a past main verb would have allowed the optative, and the future infinitive ἀναθήσειν for the promise.

sentences.t: Περιτυχὼν δὲ πήρᾳ, ἐν ᾗ ἀμύγδαλά τε ἦν καὶ φοίνικες, ταῦτα ἀνείλατο οἰόμενος ἀργύριον εἶναι.
sentences.tr: Peritychōn de pērāi, en hēi amygdala te ēn kai phoinikes, tauta aneilato oiomenos argyrion einai.
sentences.l: But having come upon a wallet, in which there were both almonds and dates, he took these up, thinking them to be silver.
sentences.n: φοίνικες are the fruit of the date-palm. πήρα is the leather wallet, the scrip a traveller or shepherd carries. περιτυγχάνω takes the dative of what one falls in with, and ἀργύριον is silver in the sense of coined money.

sentences.t: Ἐκτινάξας δέ, ὡς εὗρε τὰ ἐνόντα, ταῦτα καταφαγὼν καὶ λαβὼν τῶν τε ἀμυγδάλων τὰ κελύφη καὶ τῶν φοινίκων τὰ ὀστᾶ, ταῦτα ἐπί τινος βωμοῦ ἔθηκεν, εἰπών· « Ἀπέχεις, ὦ Ἑρμῆ, τὴν εὐχήν· καὶ γὰρ τὰ ἐντὸς ὧν εὗρον καὶ τὰ ἐκτὸς πρὸς σὲ διανενέμημαι. »
sentences.tr: Ektinaxas de, hōs heure ta enonta, tauta kataphagōn kai labōn tōn te amygdalōn ta kelyphē kai tōn phoinikōn ta osta, tauta epi tinos bōmou ethēken, eipōn· « Apecheis, ō Hermē, tēn euchēn· kai gar ta entos hōn heuron kai ta ektos pros se dianenemēmai. »
sentences.l: But having shaken it out, when he found the things inside, having eaten these up and having taken both the shells of the almonds and the stones of the dates, he set these upon an altar, saying: « You have your vow in full, Hermes: for both the inner parts of what I found and the outer parts I have shared out towards you. »
sentences.i: So he shook the wallet out, and when he saw what was in it he ate it all up, took the almond shells and the date stones, laid them on an altar and said: « You have your vow paid in full, Hermes: what I found, inside and out, I have divided with you. »
sentences.n: ἀπέχω is the receipt-word of the counting-house — 'you have it in full, the account is closed'. ὀστᾶ, properly 'bones', is the regular word for the stone of a fruit. The joke turns on the two fruits being built the opposite way round: the almond's shell is on the outside, the date's stone on the inside, so what he lays on the altar can be called, quite truthfully, 'the inner parts and the outer parts' — while everything worth eating has gone to him.

sentences.t: Πρὸς ἄνδρα φιλάργυρον διὰ πλεονεξίαν καὶ θεοὺς κατασοφιζόμενον ὁ λόγος εὔκαιρος.
sentences.tr: Pros andra philargyron dia pleonexian kai theous katasophizomenon ho logos eukairos.
sentences.l: Against a money-loving man, one who through greed outwits even the gods, the story is well-timed.
sentences.i: The story is well aimed at the miser who in his greed gets the better even of the gods by cleverness.
sentences.n: καί here is 'even': the gods too, and not only men. κατασοφίζομαι is to get the better of a thing by cleverness rather than by force — the same verb closes fable 246, of a perjury neatly divided between two mouths.
